title: A fast, validated surrogate for human longevity trials

concept.text: The innovation would be a biomarker or panel that provides an early, reliable estimate of whether an intervention will improve meaningful human health outcomes associated with aging. Researchers would measure treatment-induced changes and use them to predict later clinical effects within explicitly validated populations and intervention classes. The target is a reproducible, affordable measurement system that could shorten the wait for informative longevity-trial results.

Three capabilities must be distinguished: predicting age or future health risk, changing in response to treatment, and predicting the clinical effects caused by treatment. A marker can succeed at the first two without establishing the third. A treatment that makes a biological-age score look younger has therefore not, on that basis alone, demonstrated a health benefit. The proposed breakthrough concerns treatment-effect prediction, potentially through several complementary measures with defined uses rather than one universal aging score.

significance.text: If an earlier measurement reliably predicted later clinical treatment effects, researchers could compare interventions and reject ineffective approaches sooner within its validated domain. This could substantially accelerate evidence generation for longevity research. The supplied review connects biomarker validation with clinical translation, but it does not demonstrate how much time this proposed capability would save.

Conditional impact assessment: a useful readout within a few years could make more intervention comparisons feasible and help direct resources toward treatments with better prospects. That timing is a proposed performance goal, not a demonstrated result. Any reduction in trial duration or cost would depend on measurement expense, predictive accuracy, the clinical outcomes being forecast and the amount of continued follow-up required.

The direct advance would be faster evidence generation. It would not itself extend lifespan, establish that an effective longevity treatment exists or guarantee safety. The analogy to a substitute clinical endpoint has boundaries: successful prediction for one population, mechanism or outcome cannot automatically be transferred to another, and a surrogate should not be assumed to detect every off-target harm.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central validation challenge is to establish that early treatment-induced changes predict meaningful later clinical effects, beyond the information supplied by observational associations. The supplied 2024 review documents a need for further clinical validation. It does not establish whether this capability remains unavailable in November 2026, because the supplied material contains no subsequent freshness assessment.

Scientific barriers include determining which clinical outcomes a measure can predict, whether its relationships generalize across populations and whether interventions with different mechanisms preserve those relationships. Treatment responsiveness alone is insufficient: an intervention might alter a measured feature without producing the expected clinical benefit. A complementary panel may be needed if different measures capture different aspects of aging and health.

Engineering and statistical barriers include standardized measurement, reproducibility across settings, prespecified score formulations and independent validation. The proposed capability also requires reliable prediction of trial-level clinical effects, with uncertainty that remains useful for decisions. Affordability, acceptable prediction error and a sufficiently early readout are additional design requirements; the supplied evidence does not establish that any candidate jointly satisfies them.

current_state.text: Mahdi Moqri, Chiara Herzog, Jesse R. Poganik and colleagues’ “Validation of biomarkers of aging,” published online in Nature Medicine on 14 February 2024, DOI 10.1038/s41591-023-02784-9, reviews candidate biomarkers and the validation needed for clinical use. According to the supplied evidence review, it covers predominantly observational validation, standardization, generalizability and the need for prospective clinical studies. It does not demonstrate a surrogate meeting the proposed independent, randomized cross-trial treatment-effect prediction criterion.

The documented progress is therefore the development and evaluation of candidate measures and a clearer account of their validation requirements. Observational prediction of age or health risk is relevant groundwork, but it does not establish treatment-effect surrogacy. The review leaves open whether a single measure or multiple complementary biomarkers will prove most useful. Neither an achieved readout within a few years nor a numerical acceleration of longevity trials is established by the supplied evidence.

The supplied evidence review reports that the article’s identity was verified and its complete main text, references and affiliations were retained without reported truncation; separately hosted supplements were not supplied. Its conclusions draw on the broader article, including the clinical-validation discussion, rather than the introductory phrase cited in the earlier candidate. No conclusion here requires inspection of graphical details beyond that review.

Evidence limitation: the source index records retrieval on 11 November 2026, but retrieval of a 2024 article does not establish the field’s status in 2026. No freshness search record is supplied. The earlier research also mentions an access error for a National Institute on Aging workshop PDF, but neither that document nor an access-error record is included. Its wording and the reported access problem cannot be independently assessed from these inputs. These limitations leave later progress unresolved; they do not show that any particular result is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: prespecify the measurement method and prediction model, then validate them independently across multiple randomized trials involving different intervention mechanisms. Early biomarker changes should predict the direction and magnitude of later effects on specified clinical outcomes at the trial level. Validation should include ineffective interventions and adverse clinical effects, rather than relying only on treatments that appear beneficial. These are proposed criteria, not an established consensus standard or an achieved result.
completion_criteria.label: Independent trials validate biomarker predictions of treatment-effect direction and magnitude

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol requirements: define the populations, intervention classes, clinical endpoints, early measurement time and later follow-up period before evaluation. Set decision-relevant limits for prediction error and report uncertainty, calibration and cases where prediction fails. Explicitly test the additional claim of treatment-effect prediction rather than accepting accurate individual risk prediction or a treatment-responsive score as sufficient evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Treatment-effect prediction reports prespecified scope, error limits and uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practicality requirements: demonstrate consistent measurements and predictions across independent laboratories or clinical settings, using fixed assay procedures and score formulations. Specify acceptable measurement variability, turnaround time and cost for the intended trial setting. A panel with a restricted but useful domain could qualify; there is no requirement to reduce every aspect of aging to a single number.
completion_criteria.label: Cross-laboratory reproducibility includes specified variability, turnaround time and cost

completion_criteria.text: Proposed boundary conditions: retain direct clinical follow-up sufficient to assess prediction failures and harms that the surrogate may miss. Report exactly which outcomes, populations and intervention mechanisms have been tested, and require further validation before extending those claims. Finite studies can demonstrate breadth across the tested domain, not literal universality across all aging interventions or all possible harms.
completion_criteria.label: Clinical follow-up assesses prediction failures and harms; claims retain validated boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — LON-01, “A predictive causal theory of mammalian aging”: a causal theory could guide biomarker selection and explain when a surrogate should generalize. LON-04 instead concerns empirical validation of early treatment-effect prediction. A useful surrogate might be established within a limited domain before a comprehensive causal theory exists, while a causal theory alone would not establish clinical surrogacy.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-02, “Safe, repeatable rejuvenation of an aged human body”: a validated surrogate could help evaluate rejuvenation attempts sooner. Rejuvenation itself requires demonstrated restoration and safety; an improved biomarker reading would not establish either without the relevant validation and clinical evidence.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-03, “A validated human intervention that greatly slows systemic aging”: LON-03 concerns therapeutic efficacy, while LON-04 concerns the measurement system used to predict efficacy earlier. Trials of a slowing intervention could contribute to surrogate validation, but success with one intervention would not establish prediction across different mechanisms.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-05, “In-place repair of accumulated molecular damage in old tissues”: damage-repair interventions could be candidates for evaluation with the proposed surrogate. Measuring reduced damage would establish a different claim from showing that the reduction predicts later clinical benefit. Validation would need to connect the early measurement to the relevant outcomes.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-06, “Transfer of exceptional longevity mechanisms between species”: transferred mechanisms could motivate human interventions and candidate biomarkers. Evidence in another species would not by itself validate a human clinical surrogate; LON-04 would still require treatment-effect prediction in its intended human populations.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-07, “Control of systemic aging signals through the circulation”: circulating signals could be intervention targets, measurement inputs or both. Changing a circulating signal and validating it as a predictor of clinical treatment effects are separate achievements. A circulating marker would need its own applicability and outcome validation.

change_log.reason: The central innovation is a validated trial measurement capability, with a panel and restricted domain allowed.

change_log.reason: These are distinct evidentiary requirements; success at predicting age or responding to treatment does not establish clinical benefit.

change_log.reason: The supplied review documents a validation gap in 2024, while the absence of a freshness record leaves November 2026 status unresolved.

change_log.reason: Neither is established as an achieved property by the supplied evidence.

unresolved_issues: Whether developments after the February 2024 review established any surrogate meeting the proposed criteria remains unresolved; no freshness assessment is supplied.
The specific biomarkers or panel, clinical endpoints, populations and intervention classes remain to be selected.
Acceptable prediction error, reproducibility, readout time and cost targets require a concrete protocol; no numerical thresholds are established here.
The extent to which a candidate could predict adverse effects, and which harms would require separate monitoring, remains to be demonstrated.
The National Institute on Aging workshop’s contents and reported access error cannot be assessed from the supplied inputs; separately hosted supplements to the Nature Medicine review are also absent.

brief.title: Earlier answers about treatments for healthier aging
possible: People testing treatments for healthier aging could learn sooner whether those treatments will improve later health. An early measurement, or set of measurements, would reliably predict the health effects that longer trials would eventually reveal.
why: Researchers could compare more treatments and reject ineffective approaches sooner. That would help direct research funding and effort toward treatments with better prospects.

sources.who: Mahdi Moqri, Chiara Herzog, Jesse R. Poganik and colleagues
sources.showed: They reviewed biomarkers of aging, measurable features linked to aging and health. Most validation involved observing people rather than testing whether treatment-driven changes predict health benefits.
sources.cited_for: The review explains why predicting health risk is insufficient for predicting treatment benefits.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate an early measurement that reliably predicts treatments’ later health effects across independent trials.

sources.who: Raghav Sehgal, Albert Higgins-Chen and colleagues
sources.showed: They compared aging scores based on chemical tags on DNA across 51 intervention studies. Scores designed to predict death risk or aging speed responded most strongly to treatments.
sources.quote: clocks trained to predict mortality or pace of aging show the strongest responses across all interventions and show consistent results with one another
sources.cited_for: Some aging scores respond consistently to interventions.
sources.not_established: Responding to treatment does not establish that a score predicts the treatment’s later health benefits.

sources.showed: An analysis outside the original trial plan found that omega-3 supplements modestly slowed several DNA-based aging scores in older adults. Combined treatments added benefits on one score.
sources.quote:
Omega-3 alone slowed the DNAm 
clocks PhenoAge, GrimAge2 and DunedinPACE, and all three treatments 
had additive benefits on PhenoAge.
sources.cited_for: Treatments can change aging scores in a trial that assigns treatments by chance.
sources.not_established: The analysis does not establish that the score changes predict the treatments’ effects on later health.

sources.who: R. Waziry, C. P. Ryan and colleagues
sources.showed: An analysis outside the original trial plan found that eating fewer calories modestly slowed DunedinPACE, a DNA-based estimate of aging speed. Other aging scores did not change significantly.
sources.quote:
We found that CALERIE intervention 
slowed the pace of aging, as measured by the DunedinPACE DNAm 
algorithm, but did not lead to significant changes in biological age estimates 
measured by various DNAm clocks including PhenoAge and GrimAge.
sources.cited_for: Different aging scores can respond differently to the same treatment.
sources.not_established: Longer clinical follow-up is needed to establish whether the measured change corresponds to better health.

sources.showed: They developed DunedinPACE from long-term changes in organ health. Its blood-test measurements were repeatable and associated with disease, disability and death.
sources.quote: DunedinPACE showed high test-retest reliability, was associated with morbidity, disability, and mortality, and indicated faster aging in young adults with childhood adversity.
sources.cited_for: A repeatable blood measurement can capture differences linked to later health.
sources.not_established: Predicting who faces higher health risks does not establish prediction of treatment effects.

shown: Sehgal and colleagues have compared how aging scores respond across many human intervention studies. Together with individual trials and Belsky’s blood-test work, this establishes useful groundwork: measures can track health risk and change with treatment.
missing: Independent trials must establish that early changes predict the direction and size of later treatment effects, including failure and harm.
Predictions need defined populations, treatment types and health outcomes, with useful limits on error and uncertainty.
Measurements and predictions need consistent results across laboratories, at a practical speed and cost.
Continued health follow-up must identify prediction failures and harms the early measurement misses.

milestones.label: Independent trials confirm predictions of treatment effects
milestones.explanation: Early measurements would have to predict the direction and size of later health effects across independent trials assigning different treatments by chance. This would establish prediction of treatment effects.

milestones.label: Predictions have defined uses and error limits
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to define populations, treatments, outcomes, timing and acceptable errors in advance, then report uncertainty and failures. This would establish when predictions are useful.

milestones.label: Laboratories agree at a practical speed and cost
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would have to reproduce measurements and predictions using fixed procedures, within stated limits on variability, turnaround time and cost. This would make the system practical for trials.

milestones.label: Health follow-up reveals failures and missed harms
milestones.explanation: Continued health follow-up would have to assess prediction failures and missed harms, with claims limited to tested uses. This would establish boundaries and identify where further validation is needed.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether one measure or a complementary set will work best, and for which treatments and health outcomes.
Useful limits on prediction error, measurement variability, waiting time and cost remain to be defined.
How well early measurements could predict adverse effects, and which harms need separate monitoring, remains open.

page.title: Validated surrogate endpoints for human aging interventions
page.definition: A biomarker—a measured biological characteristic—or panel whose early treatment-induced changes predict later effects on disease, disability or survival in trials of interventions targeting human aging. Validation applies to specified populations, intervention classes and clinical outcomes.

goal.need: CALERIE randomized 220 adults for 2 years; the DO-HEALTH biomarker analysis followed 777 adults for 3 years. Both post hoc analyses detected changes in DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA. The goal is an earlier measurement that can replace waiting for clinical outcomes in a defined trial context. Biomarker responsiveness alone does not establish that substitution.

statements.quote: Validation of biomarkers of aging for use as surrogate outcomes in clinical trials is highly desirable to reduce sample numbers and trial duration.

statements.body: Representatives of the Longevity Biotechnology Association, BioAge Labs, Cambrian Bio and Juvenescence, with academic coauthors
statements.quote: ultimately support regulatory approval of biomarkers of aging as surrogate endpoints.
statements.context: The conclusion of their jointly authored recommendations identifies this as an aim of standardized biomarker collection in longevity trials.

completion.title: FDA accepts a human aging biomarker as a validated surrogate for a specified clinical benefit.
completion.criterion: A documented FDA determination accepts a biomarker or panel of biological aging as a validated surrogate endpoint for a specified later clinical benefit in trials of interventions targeting aging. The determination identifies the population, intervention context and clinical outcome, and rests on a clear mechanistic rationale and clinical evidence that treatment effects on the earlier biomarker predict that benefit. Acceptance only as a candidate or reasonably likely surrogate does not satisfy this test.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Surrogate Endpoint Resources for Drug and Biologic Development; its general validated-surrogate standard applies within a specified context of use.
completion.threshold_quote: clinical data providing strong evidence that an effect on the surrogate endpoint predicts a specific clinical benefit.
completion.basis: FDA publishes an existing evidentiary category for replacing clinical outcomes. Applying that category to biological-aging biomarkers supplies a completion test without an invented readout deadline or prediction-error cutoff. The 2024 review describes predominantly observational validation; the 21 August 2026 intervention synthesis reports responsiveness while leaving correspondence with long-term health benefits unresolved.

milestones.title: An aging-biomarker assay achieves short-term test–retest correlation of at least 0.7.
milestones.criterion: The assay achieves short-term test–retest correlation ≥0.7 in its intended human-trial setting, with standardized measurement and reproducibility across sites or laboratories. Partial evidence: on 14 January 2022, Belsky et al. reported DunedinPACE intraclass correlation 0.96 (95% CI 0.93–0.98, main text) in 36 replicate blood-DNA datasets. Technical replication does not establish repeatability across separate blood draws or laboratories.
milestones.set_by: TAME Biomarkers Workgroup, 2018 selection framework, Trial context section. The 0.7 cutoff is a trial-selection criterion, not an FDA surrogate-validation threshold.

milestones.title: An aging biomarker predicts future age-related disease independently of chronological age.
milestones.criterion: The biomarker predicts future onset of age-related conditions or diseases independently of chronological age. Belsky et al., published on 14 January 2022, reported 327 incident cardiovascular cases among 2,075 initially disease-free Framingham Offspring participants followed through 2018. The DunedinPACE hazard ratio was 1.39 per standard deviation (95% CI 1.26–1.54), adjusted for age and sex. This is prognostic evidence.
milestones.set_by: American Federation for Aging Research, Infoaging Guide to Biomarkers of Aging, published criteria; age-adjusted outcome association is also required by the TAME Biomarkers Workgroup.
milestones.threshold_quote: In other words, it must predict the future onset of age-related conditions and diseases, and do so independently of chronological age.

milestones.title: A human aging biomarker changes in response to an intervention targeting aging.
milestones.criterion: The biomarker changes in response to an intervention affecting aging biology. CALERIE's post hoc methylation analysis included 197 of 220 randomized adults: caloric restriction produced a 2–3% reduction in DunedinPACE's estimated pace of aging relative to controls over 2 years. DO-HEALTH's post hoc analysis, published on 3 February 2025, included 777 adults over 3 years; omega-3 affected PhenoAge, GrimAge2 and DunedinPACE. These are treatment-response results.
milestones.set_by: TAME Biomarkers Workgroup, 2018 selection framework, criterion 4: responsiveness to intervention.
milestones.threshold_quote: A biomarker of aging for geroscience-guided trials should be responsive to interventions that affect the biology of aging

milestones.title: Treatment effects on an aging biomarker predict clinical effects across randomized trials.
milestones.criterion: Across multiple randomized trials in a defined clinical context, treatment effects on the early aging biomarker predict effects on the later clinical endpoint. This is the IOM committee's meta-analytic approach; it sets no universal prediction-error cutoff. The 21 August 2026 synthesis of 51 intervention studies, comprising 3,128 samples, assessed responsiveness and did not establish this result.
milestones.set_by: Institute of Medicine Committee on Qualification of Biomarkers and Surrogate Endpoints in Chronic Disease, 2010 report, Chapter 2: its published meta-analytic approach to surrogate validation.
milestones.threshold_quote: For the meta-analysis approach, the average value of the surrogate measured in each trial should be able to predict the outcome for that trial.

not_found: No aging-specific maximum readout time, cost ceiling or cross-trial prediction-error cutoff was found in the FDA materials or consortium frameworks searched.
No prospective cross-trial validation establishing clinical treatment-effect prediction by an aging biomarker was identified in the papers and regulatory sources searched through 14 November 2026.
The NIA's 2022 Division of Aging Biology review report and 2021 biomarker-initiative article returned access errors.

results.finding: DunedinPACE decreased significantly in 16 interventions across 51 studies with 3,128 blood samples.
results.detail: The analysis compared pre- and post-intervention measurements. The authors describe the pooled analysis as descriptive rather than causal and note heterogeneity in study designs.
results.quote: Among all the biomarkers, DunedinPACE was the most responsive to a deflection in biological age, significantly decreasing in 16 interventions and increasing in only 1.

results.finding: In 777 DO-HEALTH participants, omega-3 reduced DunedinPACE relative to controls by 0.17 standardized units over 3 years.
results.detail: Post hoc analysis of generally healthy, active Swiss adults aged 70 or older. The long-term clinical significance of the clock changes remains unknown.
results.quote:
Daily omega-3 supplementation reduced the age-acceleration 
or pace-of-aging values of three of four clocks in our primary analysis  
(PhenoAge difference (d) = −0.16 (95% confidence interval (CI) −0.02 
to −0.30); GrimAge2 d = −0.32 (−0.06 to −0.59); DunedinPACE d = −0.17 
(−0.04 to −0.31)).

results.finding: In 197 CALERIE participants, caloric restriction reduced DunedinPACE's estimated pace of aging by 2–3% relative to controls.
results.detail: This was a post hoc analysis of a randomized trial in healthy adults over two years. Long-term clinical benefit was not established.
results.quote:
Standardized treatment effects 
on DunedinPACE correspond to a reduction in the pace of aging of 
2–3%.

results.finding: DunedinPACE showed an ICC of 0.96 in 36 replicate blood-DNA datasets.
results.detail: These were technical replicates; they do not establish repeatability across separate blood draws or reproducibility across laboratories in the intended trial setting.

results.finding: In the 2,471-person Framingham Offspring cohort, DunedinPACE predicted incident CVD with a hazard ratio of 1.39 per standard deviation.
results.detail: The CVD analysis adjusted for chronological age and sex; this is prognostic evidence.

results.finding: MRI-derived brain-age difference in 20 participants: within-scanner test–retest ICC 0.94.
results.detail: Scans were approximately four weeks apart. In 11 participants scanned across two sites, the same raw-data CNN measure had ICC 0.66. The study did not establish repeatability in an intended human-trial setting.
results.quote:
within-scanner
reliability for raw data using CNN was very high (ICC ¼ 0.94)

results.finding: In the UK Biobank cohort (n=43,616), brain proteomic age gap predicted incident all-cause dementia: HR 1.88 per standard deviation.
results.detail: The association was adjusted for chronological age and other demographic and lifestyle factors. The stated sample size is the overall cohort size.
results.quote: the brain age gap showed the strongest association with the future risk of NDs, including all-cause dementia (ACD; hazard ratio (HR) per 1-s.d. change: 1.88,

results.finding: In 958 older adults, daily multivitamin–multimineral supplementation reduced PCGrimAge's yearly increase by 0.113 years versus placebo.
results.detail: The prespecified analysis covered two years and excluded participants with major chronic disease at baseline or incident cardiovascular disease or invasive cancer during follow-up. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied; clinical relevance remains uncertain.

results.finding: In 958 COSMOS participants, DunedinPACE had a within-individual intraclass correlation of 0.818.
results.detail: Measurements were taken at baseline and annual follow-ups, rather than in a short-term test–retest study. The paper does not establish reproducibility across laboratories.
results.quote: The within-individual stability across repeated measurements was measured using intra-class correlation coefficients, with 0.937 for PCHorvath, 0.910 for PCHannum, 0.919 for PCGrimAge, 0.877 for PCPhenoAge and 0.818 for DunedinPACE.

results.finding: In 117 COSMOS participants, clock changes were estimated to mediate 4.1–5.2% of MVM-related episodic memory improvements.
results.detail: This exploratory mediation analysis was not statistically significant and involved one trial, rather than prediction of clinical effects across multiple randomized trials.
results.quote: Mediation analyses showed that changes in PCPhenoAge and PCGrimAge may mediate 4.1–5.2% of MVM-related improvements in episodic memory, but these results did not reach statistical significance.

results.finding: Brain-PAD estimates in 40 participants had within-scanner test–retest ICC >0.93 across three models.
results.detail: Participants were rescanned within four hours at one center. Reproducibility across different scanners varied, and the study does not establish reproducibility across sites or laboratories or performance in an aging-intervention trial.
results.quote: Within-scanner repeatability was excellent (ICC-AA>0.93) for all models.

results.finding: DunedinPACNI test–retest reliability in 45 participants: intraclass correlation 0.94.
results.detail: The HCP MRI test–retest result exceeds the threshold, but the text does not establish the retest interval, performance in an intended human-trial setting, or reproducibility across sites or laboratories.

results.finding: In the UK Biobank cohort (n=44,458), extreme myeloid lineage aging predicted incident type 2 diabetes (HR 3.88).
results.detail: The disease analysis covered 15 years of follow-up; Figure 4c describes hazard ratios adjusted for chronological age and sex. The exact diabetes analysis sample size is not stated in the supplied text.

results.finding: In 3,977 China Kadoorie Biobank participants, the kidney protein-based age gap predicted incident type 2 diabetes (HR 2.13).
results.detail: Age gaps were defined relative to same-aged peers. The result is prognostic evidence; it does not establish a treatment surrogate.
results.quote: Consistent with findings in UK Biobank, the kidney age gap showed broad and strong associations with incident diseases, including type 2 diabetes (HR = 2.13, 95% CI: 1.92–2.37), essential hypertension (HR = 1.34, 95% CI: 1.27–1.43), and renal failure (HR = 2.16, 95% CI: 1.61–2.91).

results.finding: In 1,031 adults, vitamin D3 reduced leukocyte telomere length attrition by 0.14 kb versus placebo over 4 years.
results.detail: The telomere study was a post hoc analysis of a randomized trial; 37.4% of measurements were missing at year 4. Omega-3 supplementation had no significant effect on telomere length.
results.quote: Compared to placebo, vitamin D3 supplementation significantly decreased LTL attrition by 0.14 kilo base pairs (kb) (95%CI: 0.007, 0.27) over 4 years (p = 0.039).
